passage: I'm Anjali, and I sit behind Elizabeth in class. During art today her bottle of blue ink tipped over and ran across Meera's library book. Elizabeth's ears went bright red. She muttered, "I'm so stupid," and then stopped, as if she had heard herself. Nobody said anything. She took a breath, walked to Meera's desk and said, "I'm sorry. That was my fault. I can help wipe the pages, and I'll tell the librarian myself." Meera pulled her book closer and looked at the page for a moment, then nodded. I couldn't tell if Elizabeth was still upset, because she kept her head down until lunch, but she did go and get the tissues.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's bottle of ink spill on?
qa.a: It spilled on Meera's library book.

qa.q: What might Elizabeth have been feeling when her ears went red and she muttered that she was stupid?
qa.a: Probably shame and worry, since her red ears and harsh words about herself suggest it, though Anjali can't be sure what Elizabeth thinks inside.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do next to settle things with Meera?
qa.a: She can keep her offer to help wipe the pages and tell the librarian, and remind herself that spilling ink was a mistake, not proof she is bad. 🙂

qa.q: How might Meera have seen the moment?
qa.a: Meera was likely upset about her book at first, but Elizabeth's quick apology and offer to help probably made it easier to accept.

grounding: Illustrates shame after spilling ink on a friend's book, then an apology and offer to fix it, seen by an observer.

passage: Note from Vandana, class teacher, Class 5B. At Friday's assembly Madhuri got stuck on the third line of her poem and kept repeating the first word. A few children laughed, then many more. Madhuri stopped, stared at the floor and left the stage quickly. Afterwards she sat in a corner of the library and told me she wished the floor would open. Her friend Tarun sat beside her without saying much and shared his tiffin. By Monday most of the class was talking about the cricket match. What I did: I spoke to the class about laughing at someone's stumble, and I offered Madhuri a private recitation, which she may decline. She told me, "Tarun didn't laugh."

qa.q: Who sat beside Madhuri in the library?
qa.a: Her friend Tarun sat beside her and shared his tiffin.

qa.q: What does Madhuri's wish that the floor would open suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests deep embarrassment and a wish to disappear from everyone's eyes.

qa.q: How could Vandana support Madhuri in the coming weeks?
qa.a: Vandana could keep the private recitation offer open without pressure and watch that classmates do not bring the moment up again.

qa.q: What might Tarun's quiet company have meant to Madhuri compared with the laughter?
qa.a: It showed her that one person was on her side. His not laughing seemed to matter more to her than the crowd's noise.

grounding: Shows a child laughed at on stage wanting to disappear, while a friend who stays beside her matters more and the class moves on.

passage: Noa had been sitting on the stairs for twenty minutes with the two halves of the broken blue bowl in her lap. Her friend Hiroshi, waiting by the door with his football, whispered, "Just tell your mum. Mine was cross for one evening, then it was over." Noa stood up and carried the pieces to the kitchen, where her mum was chopping onions. "Mum, I dropped your bowl. I'm so sorry. I was going to hide it." Her mum put the knife down. "Oh, Noa. Thank you for telling me. Are you hurt?" "No." "Then it's only a bowl. We'll see if glue works." Noa's shoulders dropped for the first time all afternoon, and she leaned against her mum.

qa.q: What did Noa carry into the kitchen?
qa.a: She carried the two halves of the broken blue bowl.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling as her talk with Mum ended?
qa.a: Relief. Her shoulders dropped for the first time all afternoon and she leaned against her mum.

qa.q: What could Noa do next to help mend things?
qa.a: She could help try the glue on the bowl, and next time tell her mum sooner instead of waiting on the stairs. 🙂

qa.q: What did Noa's mum seem to care about more than the bowl?
qa.a: She asked first whether Noa was hurt, so Noa's safety and honesty mattered to her more than the bowl.

grounding: Shows a child confessing a mistake to a mother who forgives quickly, giving relief and the sense that it can be mended.

passage: The tin roof of the village school rattled in the wind as the teacher held up Jasleen's copy. "Three times I have shown you how to carry the one, and still you forget!" Jasleen's cheeks burned. "I did try," she muttered, folding her arms over the page. Outside, a tractor droned past. When class ended she wanted to tear the sheet out. Rajni, on the same bench, slid her own copy across. "I got it wrong yesterday too." Jasleen looked at the red circle again. The carried digit sat under the wrong column. "I'm not useless," she whispered. "I just put it in the wrong place." She copied the sum again, slowly.

qa.q: What did Jasleen put in the wrong place?
qa.a: The carried digit sat under the wrong column.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen mutter "I did try" while folding her arms over the page?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and defensive, so she pulled away from the scolding to protect herself.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do next with the corrected sum?
qa.a: When she is calm she can ask the teacher to check the carrying step once more, and practise it slowly a few times.

qa.q: How might Rajni see Jasleen's reaction?
qa.a: Rajni got it wrong yesterday too, so she probably knew the sting and wanted to show a slip is common. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates being scolded sharply, feeling ashamed and defensive, then listening for what to learn without deciding one is useless.

passage: Darshan had knocked the clay water pot off the ledge while chasing the calf, and it broke into six pieces. He scooped them up and pushed them under the straw in the cowshed. At dinner Ma searched the corner where the pot always stood. "Has anyone seen it?" Darshan pushed his roti away. His elder brother Madhav glanced at him but said nothing. All night the secret sat on his chest like a stone. In the morning he found his parents on the veranda. "Ma, Papa, I broke the pot. I hid it in the cowshed. I'm sorry." Ma sighed. "I'd rather you told me at once. Come, we'll buy another on Thursday." Darshan breathed out, long and slow.

qa.q: Where did Darshan hide the pieces of the pot?
qa.a: He pushed them under the straw in the cowshed.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when he pushed his roti away at dinner?
qa.a: He felt worried and guilty. The secret sat on his chest like a stone, so he could not eat.

qa.q: What did confessing change, and what could Darshan do next time?
qa.a: It lifted the weight and showed his parents he could be trusted. Next time he could tell them right after the accident.

qa.q: How might Ma have felt when Darshan told her the truth?
qa.a: She was probably sad about the pot but glad he came forward. She did not scold him and even planned to buy another.

grounding: Shows a child who hid broken pieces, felt the secret grow heavy, and found relief in telling the truth late.

passage: At Friday talent hour in the Mumbai building's community hall, Simran opened her mouth and a clear song about the monsoon filled the room. Amandeep forgot to clap for a second. Goosebumps ran up his arm. "She's just born with it," Jatin whispered, shrugging. "No point trying to sing like that." Amandeep didn't feel that way; his chest felt wide and warm. At the bus stop he caught up with Simran. "How do you practise? Every day?" She laughed, surprised. "Ten minutes on Nani's harmonium before school. I still crack on the high notes." "Can I listen sometime?" "Come Saturday," she said. Amandeep grinned all the way home.

qa.q: Where does Simran practise, and for how long?
qa.a: She practises for ten minutes on Nani's harmonium before school.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling as Simran sang?
qa.a: Amazement and warmth. He forgot to clap, got goosebumps and his chest felt wide. 😊

qa.q: What might Amandeep do when he goes on Saturday?
qa.a: He can listen, ask what she practises, and start a small routine of his own instead of assuming he could never do it.

qa.q: How might Simran feel about Amandeep's question compared with Jatin's remark?
qa.a: Jatin's "born with it" ignores her effort, while Amandeep's question shows he values her practice. She seemed surprised and pleased.

grounding: Illustrates admiring a classmate's singing and asking how she practises rather than deciding one could never do it.

passage: Twenty minutes before the school bus left, the annual-day hall was still full of paint cans, and a power cut had switched off the fans. Everyone crowded round Sumitra's backdrop of snow peaks. "Unreal!" "Sumitra, do mine next!" Mridul stood behind them holding a brush over the blank welcome banner. He felt invisible, and his jaw tightened. "She probably traced it" rose to his tongue, but he shut his mouth on it. Why did it sting so much? Because he wanted someone to say wow to him. He knelt on the floor and began the big curly letters he had practised all term at the back of his notebook. When the bus horn sounded, the teacher stopped at the banner. "Who did this lettering?"

qa.q: Why were the fans off in the hall?
qa.a: There had been a power cut.

qa.q: Why did Mridul nearly say that Sumitra traced the backdrop?
qa.a: He felt invisible and stung by all the praise, so part of him wanted to bring Sumitra down, but he shut his mouth on it.

qa.q: What did Mridul do with his envy that helped him?
qa.a: He asked himself why it stung, saw that he wanted to be noticed for his own work, and put his effort into the lettering.

qa.q: What would change if Mridul had said the traced remark aloud?
qa.a: Sumitra would likely have felt hurt, and Mridul's own lettering might have gone unnoticed behind an argument.

grounding: Shows envy at a classmate's praised talent, felt as invisibility, turned into work on one's own strength instead of running the classmate down.

passage: Evening tea was being poured on the veranda when Harish's father tapped the newspaper. "Your cousin Ojas got first rank at the block level. Why can't you be more like Ojas? He studies properly, and you bring me middle marks." Harish stared at his steel glass. His chest felt stuffed with wet cotton. He wanted to run out to the fields. Instead he took a breath. "Papa, I do work hard, just differently from Ojas." His voice shook. "Yesterday I fixed the cycle chain by myself. Could you look at what I do too?" His father lowered the paper. His mother, at the stove, said nothing but stirred more slowly. "Show me tomorrow," his father said at last, gruffly.

qa.q: What did Ojas get at the block level?
qa.a: He got first rank at the block level.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when his chest felt stuffed with wet cotton?
qa.a: He felt crushed and hurt at being compared, and tempted to run away to the fields.

qa.q: What did Harish try that could help his father see him differently?
qa.a: He said calmly that he works hard in a different way and offered to show the cycle chain he fixed.

qa.q: How might Harish's father see the moment?
qa.a: He may worry about Harish's marks and think comparing will push him. Hearing Harish speak up made him lower the paper and agree to look tomorrow.

grounding: Illustrates a child crushed by a parent's comparison to a cousin who answers by saying he is trying his own way and asks to be noticed.

passage:
Saturday. When the judges called Lalremsiami's name for the drawing prize, the hall clapped, and warmth spread all the way to her toes. She held the small trophy tight and grinned until her cheeks ached. She wanted to hear the applause again.

Monday. In the art room she set the trophy on Shalini Ma'am's table. "Your lessons on shading did this. Thank you." Shalini Ma'am laughed. "The hand was yours." But she looked very pleased.

The next Thursday. Lalremsiami sat beside Nunpari, a younger girl who struggled with the shadow under her tree. "Lightly first, like this." On her way out she glanced at the trophy shelf and let herself enjoy it for a moment.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami win the prize for?
qa.a: She won the drawing prize.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami set the trophy on Shalini Ma'am's table?
qa.a: She wanted to thank her teacher, feeling that the shading lessons helped her win, so gratitude sat alongside her pride. 😊

qa.q: How does helping Nunpari keep Lalremsiami's pride healthy?
qa.a: Sharing what she learned turns the win into something for others, so she can enjoy the applause without looking down on anyone.

qa.q: How might Shalini Ma'am feel watching her student help a younger child?
qa.a: Probably proud and happy that what she taught is being passed on.

grounding: Shows a child proud of a prize, thanking her teacher and helping a younger learner, over three days.

passage:
"Kavitha, she's not eating," Papa murmured.
"Shalini, what's the matter?" said Amma.
"Rohan didn't even say well done," Shalini said, pushing rice around her plate. "He walked away when the teacher gave me the certificate."
"Maybe he's hurting. He wanted that quiz cup too, no?"
"But I didn't do anything wrong! Now I feel bad for winning. Should I have lost?"
"Did you cheat?"
"No!"
"Then you owe no apology for winning. But you can be kind."
Shalini thought. "I could leave him alone at lunch tomorrow. Not chase him."
"And?"
"And tell him I like sitting with him, whenever he wants. Amma, will he still be my friend?"
"Give it time."
Shalini nodded and finally took a bite.

qa.q: What did Rohan do when the teacher gave Shalini the certificate?
qa.a: He walked away.

qa.q: What is Shalini feeling about her win, and why?
qa.a: She feels confused and a bit guilty, because Rohan went cold and she wonders if she should have lost.

qa.q: What plan did Shalini make for tomorrow, and why is it a kind one?
qa.a: She will leave him alone at lunch and tell him she likes sitting with him whenever he wants. Giving space without pushing keeps the friendship open. 🙂

qa.q: What might Rohan be going through?
qa.a: He wanted the quiz cup too, so he is probably hurting and disappointed, not necessarily angry at Shalini.

grounding: Shows a child confused and guilty after a friend goes cold over her win, deciding to give space and stay kind.
